# Trailing Edge Cooling Configuration for Turbine Airfoils

## Background and Technical Challenge

Turbine airfoils operate within an exceptionally demanding thermal environment, being continuously exposed to high-temperature combustion gases as they extract energy from the working fluid. Among the various regions of an airfoil, the trailing edge presents a particularly difficult cooling challenge. Because this portion of the airfoil tapers to a comparatively thin cross-section, the physical space available for incorporating cooling structures is inherently limited. Simultaneously, the trailing edge is subjected to intense thermal loading from both the pressure and suction sides of the airfoil, making effective heat removal essential to preserving component durability and service life. Inadequate cooling in this region can lead to thermal fatigue, oxidation, and premature failure, underscoring the importance of a well-designed cooling architecture.

## Description of the Cooling Configuration

The disclosed configuration addresses these challenges through a carefully structured internal cooling arrangement that guides coolant toward and ultimately through the trailing edge. Central to this arrangement is a series of radially-elongated pins positioned within the internal cooling cavity of the airfoil. These pins are organized into multiple rows that are spaced apart from one another in the chordwise direction—that is, along the axis extending from the leading edge toward the trailing edge. The spacing and staggering of these pin rows create interspaced coolant passages through which the cooling fluid must navigate. As the coolant flows around and between the successive rows of pins, it is repeatedly disrupted and redirected, promoting turbulence and enhancing the convective heat transfer between the coolant and the surrounding metal surfaces. In this way, the pin arrangement not only serves a structural reinforcement function but also substantially increases the thermal effectiveness of the coolant as it traverses the aft portion of the airfoil.

Downstream of the final row of pins, the cooling architecture transitions into a row of axially-elongated partition walls. These partition walls extend from the region of the last pin row all the way to the trailing edge itself. Rather than being oriented radially like the pins, the partition walls are elongated in the axial direction, effectively channeling and organizing the coolant flow as it approaches the terminal edge of the airfoil.

## Coolant Discharge Arrangement

The spacing between adjacent partition walls defines a series of axial coolant exit slots. These slots receive the coolant that has been delivered by the final row of pins and provide a controlled path for that coolant to be discharged from the interior of the airfoil into the surrounding hot gas path. By directing the spent coolant through these discrete exit slots, the configuration ensures that the trailing edge region receives continuous thermal protection right up to the point of discharge. The coolant absorbs heat as it passes through the pin field and partition wall passages, and its ultimate ejection into the gas path completes the cooling circuit.

## Resulting Benefits

Taken together, this integrated arrangement of radially-elongated pins, interspaced coolant passages, axially-elongated partition walls, and axial exit slots enables effective thermal management of the airfoil's trailing edge region. The design maximizes heat extraction from a geometrically constrained area, maintains structural integrity through the reinforcing action of the pins and partition walls, and provides a reliable means of coolant discharge. The result is an airfoil trailing edge that can withstand the severe thermal conditions of turbine operation while supporting improved component longevity and overall engine performance.

# Understanding Axially Loaded Components in Engineering

The design of mechanical structures often depends on how forces are distributed throughout a system. Among the many ways loads can be applied, axial loading represents one of the most fundamental concepts that engineers must master. When a force acts along the central axis of a component, that member is said to be loaded axially, resulting in either tension or compression along its length.

Each structural element responds differently to axial forces depending on its material properties, cross-sectional area, and overall geometry. A slender column, for instance, may behave very differently from a thick, stout support even when both are subjected to identical axial loads. Understanding these differences is essential for predicting how a structure will perform under real-world conditions.

The behavior of axially loaded members follows well-established principles. When a component is pulled axially, its fibers stretch, and the material experiences tensile stress. Conversely, when pushed, the component shortens and endures compressive stress. Engineers calculate these stresses to ensure that each part remains within safe operating limits and does not fail unexpectedly.

Each application demands careful consideration of the forces involved. Bridge cables, building columns, engine connecting rods, and aircraft struts all rely on components that must withstand axial loading. The reliability of these systems depends on accurate analysis, thoughtful material selection, and rigorous testing before any design is put into service.

The importance of studying axially loaded members cannot be overstated. By analyzing how each component responds when loaded axially, engineers create safer, more efficient, and more durable structures that serve society for generations to come.

**Claim 1.** A turbine airfoil comprising:

a pressure sidewall and a suction sidewall joined together at a leading edge and a trailing edge, said pressure sidewall and said suction sidewall being spaced apart to define an internal cooling cavity therebetween;

a plurality of elongated pins disposed within said internal cooling cavity proximate said trailing edge, each of said elongated pins extending between and connecting said pressure sidewall and said suction sidewall, and each of said elongated pins having a longitudinal axis oriented generally toward said trailing edge;

a plurality of partition walls disposed within said internal cooling cavity between adjacent ones of said elongated pins, said partition walls extending between said pressure sidewall and said suction sidewall and being arranged to define a plurality of discrete coolant flow channels directing a coolant flow toward said trailing edge; and

a plurality of coolant exit slots defined at said trailing edge, each of said coolant exit slots being in fluid communication with a respective one of said coolant flow channels and configured to discharge said coolant flow from said internal cooling cavity;

wherein said elongated pins and said partition walls cooperate to meter and direct said coolant flow through said coolant flow channels to said coolant exit slots, thereby providing convective cooling of said trailing edge.

**Claim 2.** The turbine airfoil of claim 1, wherein each of said elongated pins has an elongated cross-sectional shape defining a length-to-width ratio of at least 2:1.

**Claim 3.** The turbine airfoil of claim 1, wherein said elongated pins are arranged in a plurality of staggered rows extending in a spanwise direction of said airfoil.

**Claim 4.** The turbine airfoil of claim 1, wherein said partition walls extend downstream of said elongated pins toward said trailing edge to separate said coolant flow into said discrete coolant flow channels.

**Claim 5.** The turbine airfoil of claim 1, wherein each of said coolant exit slots has a cross-sectional flow area that is smaller than a cross-sectional flow area of said respective coolant flow channel, so as to accelerate said coolant flow upon discharge.

# Turbine Airfoil Cooling Feature with Radially Arranged Pin Rows and Trailing Edge Partition Walls

## Technical Field

[0001] The present disclosure relates generally to turbine airfoils, and more particularly to a cooling arrangement for a trailing edge region of a turbine airfoil employing radially arranged pin banks and partition walls to channel coolant into a hot gas path.

## Background

[0002] Gas turbine engines operate at elevated temperatures that frequently exceed the material limits of the components exposed to the hot combustion gases. Turbine airfoils, in particular, require internal cooling to maintain structural integrity and service life. The trailing edge region presents a particular challenge due to its reduced cross-sectional thickness, which limits the available volume for internal cooling passages while still requiring adequate heat removal.

## Summary

[0003] A turbine airfoil is disclosed having an improved cooling feature in the trailing edge region that combines radially arranged rows of pins with partition walls to meter and direct coolant flow into the hot gas path, thereby improving cooling effectiveness and reducing thermal gradients.

## Detailed Description

[0004] Referring now to **FIG. 1**, a turbine airfoil **10** includes a pressure sidewall **12** and a suction sidewall **14** that are joined together at a leading edge **16** and at a trailing edge **18**. The airfoil **10** extends in a radial (spanwise) direction from a root **20** to a tip **22**, and in a chordwise direction from the leading edge **16** to the trailing edge **18**.

[0005] The pressure sidewall **12** and the suction sidewall **14** define therebetween an internal cooling cavity **24** through which a coolant **26**, such as compressor bleed air, is supplied. The coolant **26** may be delivered from a supply passage **28** disposed within the root **20** and communicating with the cooling cavity **24**.

[0006] As shown in **FIG. 2**, a trailing edge cooling region **30** is disposed proximate the trailing edge **18** and receives the coolant **26** from the internal cooling cavity **24**. The trailing edge cooling region **30** includes a plurality of pins **32** and a plurality of partition walls **40** that cooperate to channel the coolant **26** toward and through the trailing edge **18**.

### Pin Arrangement

[0007] The plurality of pins **32** extend between an interior surface **13** of the pressure sidewall **12** and an interior surface **15** of the suction sidewall **14**, spanning the internal width of the trailing edge cooling region **30**. Each pin **32** may be integrally formed with, or joined to, the sidewalls **12**, **14**, such that each pin **32** conducts heat from the sidewalls **12**, **14** into the coolant **26** and further disrupts the boundary layer of the coolant **26** flowing thereover to enhance convective heat transfer.

[0008] The pins **32** are organized into a plurality of radial rows **34a**, **34b**, **34c** (collectively **34**), each radial row **34** extending generally in the radial direction between the root **20** and the tip **22**. The radial rows **34** are arranged in chordwise succession such that the coolant **26** flows sequentially across a first radial row **34a**, then a second radial row **34b**, and then a third radial row **34c**, prior to reaching the trailing edge **18**.

[0009] In the illustrated embodiment, the pins **32** of adjacent radial rows **34** are staggered relative to one another such that a pin **32** of the second radial row **34b** is radially offset from the pins **32** of the first radial row **34a**. This staggered configuration causes the coolant **26** to follow a tortuous flow path **36**, increasing residence time and turbulence within the trailing edge cooling region **30**.

[0010] A pin diameter **D** and a chordwise pin spacing **S1** and radial pin spacing **S2** may be selected to establish a desired pressure drop and heat transfer coefficient. In certain embodiments, the ratio of radial pin spacing **S2** to pin diameter **D** is between approximately 2.0 and 3.0.

### Partition Walls

[0011] Referring to **FIG. 3**, a plurality of partition walls **40** are disposed downstream of the plurality of pins **32**, between the pins **32** and the trailing edge **18**. Each partition wall **40** extends in a generally chordwise direction and, like the pins **32**, spans between the interior surface **13** of the pressure sidewall **12** and the interior surface **15** of the suction sidewall **14**.

[0012] The partition walls **40** are spaced apart from one another in the radial direction and define therebetween a plurality of discrete discharge channels **42**. Each discharge channel **42** receives the coolant **26** from the plurality of pins **32** and directs the coolant **26** toward a corresponding trailing edge outlet **44** defined at, or proximate to, the trailing edge **18**.

[0013] The partition walls **40** serve to organize and meter the coolant **26** exiting the pin banks. Whereas the pins **32** promote lateral (radial) mixing of the coolant **26**, the partition walls **40** subdivide the coolant flow into segregated streams and reestablish a predominantly chordwise flow direction as the coolant **26** approaches the trailing edge outlets **44**. This arrangement provides substantially uniform radial distribution of the coolant **26** along the span of the trailing edge **18**.

[0014] Each discharge channel **42** may converge in the chordwise direction, having an inlet cross-sectional area **46** adjacent the pins **32** that is greater than an outlet cross-sectional area **48** adjacent the trailing edge outlet **44**. The convergence accelerates the coolant **26** as it is discharged, improving film coverage and reducing the potential for hot gas ingestion.

### Coolant Discharge into the Hot Gas Path

[0015] In operation, the coolant **26** is supplied from the supply passage **28** into the internal cooling cavity **24** and flows in a chordwise direction toward the trailing edge cooling region **30**. The coolant **26** first traverses the staggered radial rows **34** of pins **32**, where heat is convectively removed from the sidewalls **12**, **14** and transferred into the coolant **26**.

[0016] Upon exiting the plurality of pins **32**, the coolant **26** enters the discharge channels **42** defined between the partition walls **40**. The partition walls **40** channel the coolant **26** through the trailing edge outlets **44** and into a hot gas path **50** external to the airfoil **10**, wherein hot combustion gases **52** flow over the pressure sidewall **12** and the suction sidewall **14**.

[0017] The coolant **26** discharged from the trailing edge outlets **44** forms a cooling film **54** over an external surface **19** of the trailing edge **18**, thereby insulating the trailing edge **18** from the hot combustion gases **52**. In this manner, the combined action of the radial rows **34** of pins **32** and the partition walls **40** provides both internal convective cooling and external film cooling of the thermally challenged trailing edge region **30**.

[0018] In an alternative embodiment (not shown), the trailing edge outlets **44** may be configured as pressure-side bleed slots recessed into the pressure sidewall **12** proximate the trailing edge **18**, rather than as edge-discharge apertures, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

counterfactuals.output:
# Cooling Pins and Partition Walls in Turbine Blade Trailing Edge

The trailing edge of a gas turbine blade presents a unique cooling challenge because it's a thin, tapering region that experiences high thermal loads but has limited internal space. Cooling pins (pin fins) and partition walls work together to solve this problem effectively.

## Partition Walls: Directing the Flow

Partition walls (also called ribs or dividers) serve to:

- **Channel coolant** through serpentine or radial passages within the blade interior
- **Guide the flow** progressively toward the trailing edge from the mid-chord cooling cavities
- **Control the distribution** of coolant so that adequate flow reaches the thin trailing section
- **Create pressure differentials** that drive coolant through the pin-fin array and out the discharge slots

These walls essentially define the internal "roadmap" the coolant follows before reaching the trailing edge.

## Cooling Pins: Enhancing Heat Transfer

Pin fins are small cylindrical (or sometimes tapered/oblong) posts that bridge the pressure-side and suction-side internal walls in the narrow trailing edge cavity. They work by:

- **Increasing surface area** for convective heat transfer in a space too thin for other cooling schemes
- **Promoting turbulence** as coolant flows around them, breaking up the thermal boundary layer
- **Providing structural support** by tying the two walls together, which improves mechanical rigidity in this thin region
- **Enhancing mixing** to ensure more uniform temperature distribution

The pins are typically arranged in **staggered or in-line arrays**, with staggered configurations generally offering better heat transfer due to enhanced flow disruption.

## Working Together: The Complete System

The integrated process typically follows these steps:

1. **Supply** – Coolant (bled from the compressor) enters through internal feed passages defined by partition walls
2. **Routing** – Partition walls direct the flow toward the trailing edge cavity, controlling flow rate and pressure
3. **Heat absorption** – As coolant enters the pin-fin array, the pins boost turbulence and heat transfer, extracting thermal energy from the hot trailing edge walls
4. **Discharge** – The heated coolant exits through **trailing edge slots, holes, or cutbacks**, often providing additional film cooling on the external surface as it leaves

## Discharge Configurations

Common trailing edge ejection methods include:

- **Pressure-side cutback slots** – coolant exits along the pressure surface, adding film protection
- **Trailing edge holes** – discrete ejection points
- **Central discharge slots** – coolant exits at the very edge

The pressure-side cutback is often preferred because it maintains a sharper aerodynamic edge while still providing film cooling.

## Key Design Trade-offs

Engineers must balance:

- **Cooling effectiveness** vs. **aerodynamic losses** (thicker trailing edges cool better but hurt efficiency)
- **Coolant consumption** vs. **engine performance** (more coolant means less air for combustion/thrust)
- **Pressure drop** across the pin array vs. adequate discharge momentum

---

Would you like me to go deeper into any specific aspect—such as pin-fin heat transfer correlations, specific discharge geometries, or the aerodynamic implications of trailing edge cooling?

# Trailing Edge Cooling Arrangement of a Turbine Airfoil

The trailing edge is one of the most challenging regions to cool in a turbine airfoil due to its thin geometry, high external heat loads, and structural constraints. A typical cooling arrangement integrates several coordinated features:

## Pin Arrangement (Pin-Fin Array)

- **Pin banks** consist of short cylindrical (or shaped) pins spanning the pressure and suction side walls in the narrow trailing edge cavity.
- They are typically arranged in **staggered rows** to maximize turbulence, flow mixing, and surface area contact.
- The pins serve a **dual purpose**: they enhance convective heat transfer (acting as heat-conducting fins) and provide **structural support**, tying the two airfoil walls together for mechanical rigidity.
- Pin diameter, spacing, and density are tailored to balance heat transfer against pressure loss.

## Coolant Passages

- Cooling air is supplied from the **compressor** and enters through the airfoil root (dovetail/fir-tree).
- Internal **serpentine or radial passages** feed the trailing edge region, often as the last leg of a multi-pass circuit.
- The coolant absorbs heat as it flows aft, then is directed toward the trailing edge for discharge.

## Partition Walls (Ribs/Dividers)

- **Partition walls (ribs)** divide the internal cavity into discrete channels or metering sections.
- They **control and distribute** the coolant flow spanwise, ensuring uniform coverage and preventing localized hot spots.
- These walls often **meter the flow**, regulating pressure and mass flow into different regions of the trailing edge.

## Exit Slots (Discharge Features)

- The coolant is ejected through **exit slots or holes** at or near the trailing edge.
- Two common configurations:
  - **Pressure-side bleed slots (cutback design):** slots on the pressure surface upstream of the edge, leaving a thin lip; this provides **film cooling** over the trailing edge.
  - **Edge discharge slots:** ejection directly at the very trailing edge.
- Slots may include **lands (landings)** between them for structural continuity and to guide the ejected flow.

## Summary of Flow Path

Coolant enters the root → travels through internal serpentine/radial passages → is metered by partition walls → passes through the staggered pin-fin array (gaining maximum heat pickup) → and is finally discharged through trailing edge exit slots, providing both internal convective cooling and external film protection.

If you'd like, I can provide a labeled schematic description or discuss specific design trade-offs (e.g., pin shape optimization or slot cutback geometry).

# Trailing Edge Cooling Structure Description

The trailing edge cooling structure of the turbine airfoil incorporates an intricate arrangement of internal features designed to manage coolant flow and enhance heat transfer in this thermally critical region. As coolant travels toward the trailing edge, it first encounters an array of **pins (22a-l)**, which are cylindrical or teardrop-shaped protrusions spanning the internal cavity between the pressure and suction side walls. These pins serve dual purposes: they provide structural rigidity to the thin trailing edge section while simultaneously acting as turbulators that disrupt the coolant boundary layer, increasing turbulence and convective heat transfer as the coolant flows past and around them.

Downstream of the pin array, the coolant is channeled by a series of **partition walls (26)**, which divide the flow into discrete, organized streams. These partition walls direct and meter the coolant, ensuring uniform distribution across the span of the airfoil and preventing flow maldistribution that could create localized hot spots. The partition walls form the boundaries of individual flow passages that guide coolant toward the discharge points.

Finally, the coolant is expelled from the airfoil through **exit slots (28)** located at the trailing edge. These slots discharge the spent cooling air into the hot gas path, and in doing so, provide a degree of film cooling along the trailing edge surface. The combination of pin-fin heat transfer augmentation, partition-wall flow control, and slot discharge creates an efficient cooling scheme that maintains acceptable metal temperatures in the trailing edge—one of the most difficult regions to cool due to its thin geometry and limited coolant supply.
